title: Jeremiah 30:12–24
context: The LORD addresses Zion as a wounded woman: her hurt is incurable, no one pleads her cause, her lovers (commonly read as the foreign allies she trusted, compare 2:36; 4:30) have forgotten her, and the LORD says he struck her for the greatness of her iniquity (30:12–15). The language recalls earlier laments over the incurable wound (compare 8:22; 10:19; 15:18). Then the oracle turns: those who devour her will be devoured, and the LORD will restore her health “because they have called you an outcast” (30:16–17). In 30:18–22 he promises to rebuild Jacob’s tents, the city on its own hill and the palace in its place, with thanksgiving, growth, honor, and a ruler from among the people whom the LORD will cause to draw near to him; many readers in both traditions hear that ruler messianically, and others stress first a restored native leadership. The covenant formula follows (30:22; compare 7:23; 11:4; 24:7; 31:33). The storm of 30:23–24 repeats much of 23:19–20 with differences in wording, named here without harmonizing. On the LORD wounding his people with “the wound of an enemy,” the existing box at Judges 9:23 on God and hostile agents covers the question and is not repeated here.

verses.text: For the LORD says, “Your hurt is incurable. Your wound is grievous.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Your hurt is incurable. Your wound is grievous.” Arminian readers hear an honest diagnosis: Judah’s sin has brought a wound no human remedy can heal, which strips away false hope and prepares the people to look to God alone for healing (30:17).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same verdict as a picture of human helplessness under sin, so that healing, when it comes, will be seen as sovereign grace. Shared ground: both traditions read “incurable” as incurable by any human means, not beyond God’s power, since he promises healing a few verses later (30:17; compare 8:22).

verses.text: There is no one to plead your cause, that you may be bound up. You have no healing medicines.
verses.arminianNotes: “There is no one to plead your cause … You have no healing medicines.” Arminian readers see the loss of every advocate and remedy as the bitter fruit of choices Judah made, and they note that the absence of a human advocate makes room for the LORD himself to take up her cause.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same emptiness and often connect it with the need for a divine advocate, a role many in this tradition finally see fulfilled in Christ. Shared ground: both traditions hear the verse as lament over a people without help, and both read it as preparing for the LORD’s own intervention in 30:17.

verses.text: All your lovers have forgotten you. They don’t seek you. For I have wounded you with the wound of an enemy, with the chastisement of a cruel one, for the greatness of your iniquity, because your sins were increased.
verses.arminianNotes: “All your lovers have forgotten you … I have wounded you with the wound of an enemy … for the greatness of your iniquity.” Arminian readers see the allies Judah trusted abandoning her and God’s judgment as a just response to persistent, freely chosen sin, a discipline that still aims at her return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the one who wounds, using the enemy as his instrument while Judah remains responsible for her sins; the existing box at Judges 9:23 covers that question. Shared ground: both traditions read the “lovers” as false supports, commonly foreign allies, and both see the judgment as deserved, not arbitrary.

verses.text: Why do you cry over your injury? Your pain is incurable. For the greatness of your iniquity, because your sins have increased, I have done these things to you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Why do you cry over your injury? Your pain is incurable … I have done these things to you.” Arminian readers hear a call to honest self-examination: crying over the pain without facing its cause is not yet repentance, and the LORD names the cause plainly so that the people may turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear God owning the judgment as his act, so that suffering is not random but purposeful, and they see repentance as the fruit of grace that teaches the sinner to see sin behind the pain. Shared ground: both traditions read the repeated “greatness of your iniquity” (30:14–15) as the reason for the wound, and both see the LORD speaking in order to heal.

verses.text: Therefore all those who devour you will be devoured. All your adversaries, everyone of them, will go into captivity. Those who plunder you will be plunder. I will make all who prey on you become prey.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore all those who devour you will be devoured … I will make all who prey on you become prey.” Arminian readers see God’s justice reaching the nations that exceeded their role, so that the instruments of judgment are themselves accountable for their cruelty and pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD governing the nations, using them and then judging them, without making them less responsible for their violence. Shared ground: both traditions read the reversal as justice and as comfort for the oppressed, and both note the pattern of judgment on the nations found elsewhere in Jeremiah (compare 25:12–14; 50:17–18).

verses.text: For I will restore health to you, and I will heal you of your wounds,” says the LORD, “because they have called you an outcast, saying, ‘It is Zion, whom no man seeks after.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will restore health to you, and I will heal you of your wounds … because they have called you an outcast.” Arminian readers see the LORD’s compassion stirred by the contempt of the nations, a love that takes up the cause of the despised and invites them to trust his healing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the turn from “incurable” (30:12) to “I will heal” as grace that rests entirely on God’s initiative and his concern for his own name and people. Shared ground: both traditions read the healing as the answer to the hopeless diagnosis of 30:12–15, and both hear the taunt “It is Zion, whom no man seeks after” answered by the LORD who seeks her.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Behold, I will reverse the captivity of Jacob’s tents, and have compassion on his dwelling places. The city will be built on its own hill, and the palace will be inhabited in its own place.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises to reverse the captivity of Jacob’s tents, have compassion on his dwellings, and rebuild the city on its own hill and the palace in its place. Arminian readers see compassion that restores ordinary homes as well as public places, and many take “its own hill” as a mound of former ruins, though that detail is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same compassion as the root of restoration, with the city rebuilt where it fell as a sign that God’s purpose was not defeated by the exile. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as restoration of the community’s life, and both connect it with the return and with later hopes of renewal (compare 31:38–40).

verses.text: Thanksgiving will proceed out of them with the voice of those who make merry. I will multiply them, and they will not be few; I will also glorify them, and they will not be small.
verses.arminianNotes: “Thanksgiving will proceed out of them … I will multiply them … I will also glorify them.” Arminian readers see gratitude as the fitting response of a restored people, and they note that God’s blessing reverses the shame and diminishment of exile, inviting joyful worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the one who multiplies and glorifies, so the people’s honor is a gift and their thanksgiving gives glory back to him. Shared ground: both traditions read the joy as the reversal of the silenced songs of judgment (compare 7:34; 16:9; 33:11), and both see growth and honor as covenant blessing.

verses.text: Their children also will be as before, and their congregation will be established before me. I will punish all who oppress them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Their children also will be as before, and their congregation will be established before me. I will punish all who oppress them.” Arminian readers see the restoration of family and worshiping community, and God’s promise to defend the vulnerable against oppressors who exploit them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God establishing his congregation “before me,” so its stability rests on his presence and protection rather than on political strength. Shared ground: both traditions hear the verse as a picture of a restored, secure people of God, and both see the promise to punish oppressors as justice for the weak.

verses.text: Their prince will be one of them, and their ruler will proceed from among them. I will cause him to draw near, and he will approach me; for who is he who has had boldness to approach me?” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Their prince will be one of them … I will cause him to draw near, and he will approach me.” Arminian readers note the end of foreign rule and the promise of a ruler with access to God. Many hear a messianic hope here, while recognizing that the verse first speaks of native leadership after exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the ruler draws near because the LORD causes him to, since no one dares approach on his own; many hear a priestly-royal figure fulfilled in Christ (compare Psalm 110:4). Shared ground: readers in both traditions commonly hold the messianic reading with care, and both see access to God as his gift rather than human boldness.

verses.text: “You shall be my people, and I will be your God.
verses.arminianNotes: “You shall be my people, and I will be your God.” Arminian readers hear the covenant relationship restored, a mutual bond in which God gives himself to his people and calls them to live as his own in grateful loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same formula as a promise God guarantees, which will reach its fullest expression in the new covenant (31:33). Shared ground: both traditions read the covenant formula as the heart of the restoration, and both note how often Jeremiah uses it (compare 7:23; 11:4; 24:7; 32:38).

verses.text: Behold, the LORD’s storm, his wrath, has gone out, a sweeping storm; it will burst on the head of the wicked.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, the LORD’s storm, his wrath, has gone out, a sweeping storm; it will burst on the head of the wicked.” Arminian readers see judgment on the wicked as part of the promise: restoration for God’s people does not mean indifference to evil, and the storm warns all who persist in wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the storm as certain judgment. This verse repeats much of 23:19, where the storm is “whirling” rather than “sweeping,” and readers note the reuse without harmonizing the wording. Shared ground: both traditions read the storm as the LORD’s righteous wrath against the wicked, set beside mercy to his people.

verses.text: The fierce anger of the LORD will not return until he has accomplished, and until he has performed the intentions of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The fierce anger of the LORD will not return until he has accomplished … the intentions of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it.” Arminian readers see God’s purposes in judgment carried through, and they read the promise of later understanding as encouragement to trust when present events are dark.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD accomplishing the intentions of his heart without fail, and note that the meaning of his acts becomes clear only afterward. This verse repeats much of 23:20 with differences in wording, named here without harmonizing. Shared ground: both traditions read “the latter days” as the time when God’s purpose will be understood.
